posture_reason: nothing to protect against yet (protection is middling)
reasons: Red: Weakest-borrower risk premium, Breadth of the market
Amber: AI stocks vs their recent highs, Most fragile AI companies
Regime: credit-tail — one corner of the credit market is strained (the weakest borrowers, or a single fund or asset class) while lenders broadly stay calm — watch, not yet the serious kind
Protection posture: No action implied — nothing to protect against yet (protection is middling). (Your own rules, applied mechanically — not advice.)
Cost of protection (not part of the score): Cost of crash insurance — expensive, Cost of insurance overall — middling, Cost of Nasdaq crash insurance — middling

indicators.label: Junk-bond risk premium
indicators.detail: The extra yield lenders demand to lend to risky companies rather than to the government: 3.14%, -0.13 points over the past week. Lenders are getting nervous above 4.5%, or on a jump of more than 0.30 points in a week. A fast jump is the earliest reliable warning signal here.

indicators.label: Safe-borrower risk premium
indicators.detail: The same measure for financially solid companies: 0.86%. It barely budges in normal times, so any real move means the worry has spread beyond the risky end of the market. Nervous above 1.3%. Both ends calm (risky borrowing costs 3.7× the solid kind, which is normal).

indicators.label: Weakest-borrower risk premium
indicators.detail: The same measure for the shakiest borrowers of all: 13.07%. This is the closest free stand-in for the debt-funded AI buildout, and trouble usually shows up here before anywhere else. Nervous above 10.0%.

indicators.label: Junk bonds vs government bonds
indicators.detail: Are investors dumping risky bonds and buying safe government ones? This is priced continuously through the trading day, so it moves before the official spread figures, which arrive a day late. A fall of 1.5% or more over two weeks is the warning.

indicators.label: Bank loans to risky companies
indicators.detail: These loans pay a floating interest rate, so their price moves on worry about the companies rather than on interest-rate swings — a cleaner read on company health than bonds give you. Moving in step with junk bonds (-0.1 points over two weeks).

indicators.label: Overnight cash squeeze
indicators.detail: What banks pay to borrow cash overnight, against what the Fed pays them to leave it parked. Normally near zero or a little below; currently +4 basis points (a basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point). Staying above +8 means cash is getting scarce in the banking system.

indicators.label: Cash squeeze severity
indicators.detail: Two checks that tell a real cash shortage from the routine month-end and quarter-end noise. First, the gap between what the most desperate borrowers pay and what a typical one pays: 13 basis points, where 30 or more is unusual. Second, the Fed's standing emergency lending window — banks have barely touched it over the last three days, which is what calm looks like. Ordinary calendar spikes show neither, which is why both have to agree before this counts as stress.

indicators.label: Overall borrowing conditions
indicators.detail: A weekly summary from the Chicago Fed of how easy it is to borrow across the whole economy. Above zero means tighter than the historical average. It moves slowly, so it carries little weight here.

indicators.label: Fear now vs fear later
indicators.detail: Investors normally expect more turbulence three months out than today, which keeps this below 1.00. Above 1.00 the market is pricing the trouble as happening now — a confirmation that something is already underway, worth days of warning at most rather than weeks.

indicators.label: Cost of crash insurance
indicators.detail: How pricey insurance against a big fall is compared with ordinary options: 151, where 145 or more counts as expensive. VVIX 98 measures how pricey it is for that insurance to pay off explosively rather than merely well (expensive above 110). Protection is pricey — you would be paying up for exactly the outcome you want to insure against. This can read expensive in a perfectly calm market: it is about the price of insurance, not the odds of a crash, which is why it is not part of the score.

indicators.label: Cost of insurance overall
indicators.delta: pricier than 66% of the year · Nasdaq
indicators.detail: Priced on the Nasdaq. Two ways to check. The turbulence the market expects is running at 25.2, higher than 66% of the past year (expensive above 80%). And shares have actually been moving about 20.0, so you would be paying +5.2 points for turbulence that has not arrived (expensive above 8). This is a rough market-wide guide — check the price of the specific option before buying. Not part of the score.

indicators.label: Cost of Nasdaq crash insurance
indicators.detail: Read straight off the QQQ option chain (expiry 2026-11-27, 29 days): a put 25% likely to pay costs 26.0% implied volatility against 19.4% for the mirror-image call — +6.6 points more for downside than upside (expensive above 9). Relative to at-the-money (22.5%) that is ×1.16 (expensive above 1.4). Nasdaq downside insurance is middling in price. This is the price of the actual instrument, not an S&P proxy. Not part of the score.

indicators.label: AI stocks vs their recent highs
indicators.detail: An equal-weight basket of 14 AI-exposed companies, currently 11.6% below its three-month high, having moved -2.4% over the past two weeks. Equal-weight means a small company counts as much as a giant one, so a single megacap cannot mask the rest.

indicators.label: Most fragile AI companies
indicators.detail: CoreWeave and Oracle stand for the debt-funded end of the AI buildout. What their own lenders charge them is not published for free, so we watch for sharp share-price falls, or a sudden jump in how much the shares swing day to day, as the stand-in.

indicators.label: Breadth of the market
indicators.detail: When gains narrow to a handful of giant companies the market gets fragile. Two checks: the average US stock against the big-company index (+4.5% over the past month), and how much of the AI basket is still above its 50-day average (21%). A slow background signal, so it carries little weight.

indicators.label: Yield curve
indicators.detail: Long-term government borrowing costs minus short-term. When it goes negative — short-term paying more than long — a downturn has often followed, but 6 to 18 months later, which is no use for timing. Capped so it can never trigger a red on its own.

menu.name: Outright put ~5% below
menu.covers: losses below 670 (-5.2%), no cap on recovery
menu.gives_up: the full premium if QQQ stays above the strike
menu.explainer: Plain insurance. You pay the premium; below the strike the put pays you dollar for dollar, with no limit on how far — it behaves the same at −15% and at −50%. Above the strike it expires worthless and the premium is the cost of having been wrong. No cap on your upside. The real cost is time: rolling this every month is roughly 12–13% of the sleeve a year, which is why the posture only points here when the odds are elevated and the price is fair.
menu.scenario_note: Illustrative $100,000 sleeve held to expiry (~30 days); options settle at intrinsic value; mid prices, no commissions.
menu.fit_label: Not called for by your rules
menu.fit_why: posture is hold (credit-tail, protection is middling) — listed so you can see the price

menu.name: Outright put ~10% below
menu.covers: losses below 635 (-10.2%) — a crash, not a dip
menu.gives_up: the first ~10% of any fall, plus the premium
menu.explainer: Crash insurance, not dip insurance. Half the price of the 5% put because you absorb the first ~10% of any fall yourself; below that, unlimited protection and no cap on upside. It does nothing in an ordinary correction and everything in a collapse — the structure most aligned with a credit-driven cascade, and useless if the move stops at −8%.
menu.scenario_note: Illustrative $100,000 sleeve held to expiry (~30 days); options settle at intrinsic value; mid prices, no commissions.
menu.fit_label: Not called for by your rules
menu.fit_why: posture is hold (credit-tail, protection is middling) — listed so you can see the price

menu.name: Put spread ~5% → ~15% below
menu.gives_up: protection below 600; the sold put recovers 21% of the premium
menu.explainer: A correction hedge. You buy the 5%-below put and sell a 15%-below put, so the sold leg recovers part of the premium. Fully protected between −5% and −15%; below −15% you fall with the market again, just better off by the band. No cap on upside. Cheaper than the outright put precisely because it sells away the crash protection — the wrong structure for the scenario this tool is built to catch, the right one when lenders are calm and the move is a dip.
menu.scenario_note: Illustrative $100,000 sleeve held to expiry (~30 days); options settle at intrinsic value; mid prices, no commissions.
menu.fit_label: Not called for by your rules
menu.fit_why: posture is hold (credit-tail, protection is middling) — listed so you can see the price

menu.name: Put spread ~10% → ~25% below
menu.covers: the band 530–635 (-25% to -10%) — a crash, not a dip
menu.gives_up: the first ~10% of any fall and everything below 530
menu.explainer: The crash-band version of the spread. You buy the 10%-below put and sell a 25%-below put: nothing happens in a dip, then full protection from −10% to −25%, then you fall with the market again below that. It skips the correction the 5→15 spread insures and covers the zone where that one runs out — the coherent spread for a credit-cascade thesis, and dead weight if the move stops at −8%. Cheap because both legs are far from the money.
menu.scenario_note: Illustrative $100,000 sleeve held to expiry (~30 days); options settle at intrinsic value; mid prices, no commissions.

menu.name: Outright put ~5% below, ~92 days
menu.covers: losses below 672 (-4.9%) for ~92 days — ≈0.79% of notional per month
menu.gives_up: a quarter's premium up front; resale value if you stop needing it
menu.explainer: The same 5%-below put, bought three months out instead of one. It costs more per contract but much less per month of coverage, and it sidesteps the trap the backtest keeps showing: having to roll monthly, at prices that spike exactly when you want to keep the protection. The honest cost is that you commit the premium for a quarter — if the danger passes in two weeks you own insurance you no longer want (though it will still have resale value). No cap on upside.
menu.scenario_note: Illustrative $100,000 sleeve held to expiry (~92 days); options settle at intrinsic value; mid prices, no commissions.
menu.fit_label: Not called for by your rules
menu.fit_why: posture is hold (credit-tail, protection is middling) — listed so you can see the price

menu.name: Collar: put ~5% below, sell call ~10% above
menu.explainer: A collar with room to run. Put 5% below, financed by selling a call 10% above rather than 5%: you keep the first 10% of a rally and give up only what is beyond that. Costs more than the 5/5 collar because the farther call brings in less premium, but on a Nasdaq sleeve — where the upside lives — the extra headroom is usually the point. Floor at −5%, no limit.
menu.scenario_note: Illustrative $100,000 sleeve held to expiry (~30 days); options settle at intrinsic value; mid prices, no commissions.

menu.fit_why: posture is hold (credit-tail, protection is middling) — listed so you can see the price

menu.name: Collar: put ~5% below, sell call ~5% above
menu.explainer: Cheap protection paid for with your upside. You buy the 5%-below put and sell a 5%-above call; when implied vol is rich the call pays for most of the put. Floor at −5% with no limit, but every gain above +5% until expiry goes to the call buyer. The cap is the real cost and it is invisible until the month the market rallies — on a Nasdaq sleeve, that is where the upside lives.
